summary: An update on NETRJS, the private remote job entry protocol that UCLA's Campus Computing Network published in RFC 189 and provided to the network for over two years. NETRJS gives network access to CCN's RJS software. It was replaced by RFC 740.

plainLanguage.summary: NETRJS let network users submit batch jobs to UCLA-CCN's Remote Job Service. This update describes changes to its server, behavior, and protocol details after the service had been in use for more than two years.

questions: remote job entry on the arpanet
how did netrjs prevent lost output
what were the netrjs timeout rules
subtitle: An update to UCLA-CCN's remote job entry service and protocol.

tldr.problem: After more than two years of NETRJS use, implementations exposed protocol ambiguities and the service needed changes to its server behavior.
tldr.mechanism: The update describes a rewritten server, revised socket assignments, timeout rules, clarified protocol details, terminal options, and a fix that waits for confirmation before discarding output.
tldr.outcome: The RFC reports 1,373 jobs processed through NETRJS during October 1973. RFC 740 later replaced it.

today: RFC 599 was replaced by RFC 740. It documents a 1973 update to the NETRJS service, including reliability changes and clarified protocol behavior.

sections.title: NETRJS in Use
sections.content: NETRJS provided a network interface to UCLA-CCN's RJS, a remote job service. RFC 599 reports that the service had been available to the network for over two years and lists implementations at several sites. In October 1973, CCN processed 1,373 batch jobs through NETRJS.
sections.plainLanguage: NETRJS let users send batch jobs to UCLA-CCN for processing. This update reports how the service had been used and what its new version changed.

sections.title: Server Changes and Clarifications
sections.content:
The revised server addresses a data-loss problem called “squish.” It now waits for an RFNM (Ready for Next Message) for the end-of-data mark before telling RJS to discard job output. It also introduces a three-minute signon timeout and five-minute data-transfer timeouts, revises messages, and lets a user send Control-C to end a session.

The RFC moves NETRJS initial-contact sockets from 11, 13, and 15 to 71, 73, and 75, while allowing use of either set during the transition. It clarifies details such as record formatting, accepted user data-transfer sockets, and character mappings.
sections.plainLanguage: The new server waits for confirmation before it discards completed output, addressing a case where output could be lost. It also closes inactive sessions and clarifies how clients connect and exchange data.

sections.title: Terminal Options and User Notes
sections.content:
When defining a virtual remote batch terminal, users could choose truncated or compressed printer and punch output, automatic job resubmission after a system coldstart, automatic output restart after a broken connection, password protection, and suppression of separator cards and pages. The RFC states defaults for these choices.

It also warns that the commonly available Tenex RJS program used an older socket and character mapping, did not recognize one end-of-line character, and silently truncated card images longer than 80 characters.
sections.plainLanguage: Users could choose how output was formatted and how jobs restarted after interruptions. The RFC also documents limitations in one Tenex client program.

sections.title: Status of NETRJS
sections.content: The RFC presents itself as an update to the NETRJS specification and records changes made after operational experience. The unit metadata identifies RFC 740 as its replacement.
sections.plainLanguage: This document updates an earlier NETRJS specification. RFC 740 later replaced it.

references.text: Braden, R., "Interim NETRJS Specifications", RFC 189, July 1971.
